input.title: The Hand That Drew It: Remembering Teodora Quist
paragraphs: Teodora Quist kept a jar of eraser crumbs on her drafting table and told every new apprentice that it was the most honest record of her career.
She died last month in Lower Marrow at eighty-one, in the house behind the county survey office where she had drawn maps for forty-three years.
She taught a generation of us that a map is not a picture of the world.
It is a case made about the world, built with the same tools as any other case: selection, emphasis, and omission.
Most people would say a map is a drawing that shows where things are.
Quist would say it is a drawing that shows which things the mapmaker decided you should know are there.
A sheet of paper cannot hold a county; it holds perhaps a thousandth of what a county contains, and the rest must be left off.
Every blank space, she liked to say, is a verdict.
The road drawn thick and the stream drawn thin, the village named and the settlement unnamed, the boundary inked solid and the boundary left dotted: these are not observations but rulings.
The clearest demonstration came when the Marrow County Board asked her office for a map to accompany a vote on building along the river's lower terrace.
Standard practice would have been to shade the floodplain in the pale blue the state style guide recommended, a blue so gentle it reads as decoration.
Quist shaded it in a mud brown no one could mistake for ornament, and she printed the crest of the 1961 flood at every bridge.
The developers' attorney called the map inflammatory.
She answered that the pale blue was also inflammatory; it simply inflamed in the other direction.
The board voted nine to two against the project, and three members later said the brown was what they remembered when they voted.
Her critics, and she had them, said this proved she was an advocate who happened to own a drafting pen rather than a surveyor who happened to have opinions.
I will grant them half of that.
She did want the project stopped, and she said so to anyone who asked.
But the charge assumes that somewhere a map exists with no advocate behind it, a sheet that merely reports, and in forty-three years she never saw one and neither have I.
The pale blue floodplain had an advocate too; he was just quieter about it.
What distinguished Quist was not that her maps argued but that she signed the argument.
She trained apprentices with a single exercise, repeated until it became reflex.

Given one set of survey data for a single square mile, we drew three maps: one for a family thinking of buying a house there, one for a company planning a pipeline, and one for a child who would walk to school along its lanes.
The data never changed.
The maps never matched.
The buyer's map grew contour lines and drainage; the pipeline's map grew easements and bedrock; the child's map grew crossings, dogs, and the one hedge you could cut through.
After the third round, nobody could say "just the facts" with a straight face, which was, I think, the whole point.
The week after she died I went to the survey office, mostly to sit in the chair, and the jar of eraser crumbs was still there, fuller than I remembered.
It struck me that she had kept it because it was, in its way, her finest map: a record of every line she had chosen, on reflection, not to let stand.
We will mourn her, and we will do it properly.
But I would ask anyone reading this, the next time a map is unfolded at a council meeting or on a phone screen, to do what she did and look first for the hand that drew it.
Ask what it was told to show you.
Then ask what it was told to leave out.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the writer's inclusion of the child's map, with its "crossings, dogs, and the one hedge you could cut through," primarily speaks to the audience by

options.text: offering a homely, easily pictured example that makes vivid how what counts as relevant depends entirely on who will use the map
options.label: correct
options.why: The three maps are drawn from identical data for different users; the child's map, with its small concrete features, is the most immediately recognizable instance of relevance changing with audience, which is the lesson stated in the surrounding sentences.

options.text: appealing to readers' tenderness toward children in order to soften the harshness of the critics' charge quoted in the previous paragraph
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The detail serves the exercise's lesson about audience-dependent content; nothing in paragraph 5 revisits or softens the critics' accusation, which paragraph 4 already answered.

options.text: implying that maps drawn for children are more truthful than maps drawn for companies seeking easements and bedrock
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The paragraph treats all three maps as equally valid responses to the same data; it ranks none of them as more truthful.

options.text: demonstrating the technical precision Quist demanded in rendering very small features such as hedges and crossings
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The point is not draftsmanship or precision but selection; the features are notable because they appear on one map and not the others, not because they are finely drawn.

items.stem: The statement in paragraph 3 that "three members later said the brown was what they remembered when they voted" functions primarily as

options.text: evidence that a single design choice shaped the board's decision, supporting the claim that maps make a case rather than merely report
options.label: correct
options.why: The members' testimony links the color choice directly to the outcome, which is exactly what the thesis in paragraph 1 and the definition in paragraph 2 assert about selection and emphasis.

options.text: a claim that the board reached the correct decision in rejecting construction on the river's lower terrace
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer never judges whether the vote was right; the sentence reports what members remembered, not whether the project deserved rejection.

options.text: evidence that Quist knowingly misled the board by exaggerating the danger of flooding along the terrace
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage presents the brown shading and the printed flood crest as accurate data made emphatic, and paragraph 4 explicitly denies that emphasis equals deception.

options.text: a concession that the developers' attorney was right to call the map inflammatory in its coloring
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Quist's reply in the preceding sentence turns the charge around rather than conceding it, and the vote detail is offered as proof of effect, not as an admission.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the writer's admission "I will grant them half of that" primarily serves to

options.text: accept that Quist held a position on the project while rejecting the premise that any map can lack an advocate, shifting the issue to openness
options.label: correct
options.why: The next sentences grant that she wanted the project stopped, then deny that a map without an advocate exists, and the paragraph ends by relocating her distinction to the fact that she signed the argument.

options.text: acknowledge that the critics were correct in judging Quist unqualified to serve as a surveyor for the county
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The half granted concerns only her wish to stop the project; the writer concedes nothing about her qualifications and the passage records forty-three years of county work.

options.text: weaken the writer's own standing by confessing that personal loyalty has biased this account of her career
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The concession is about Quist's stance, not the writer's loyalty; it strengthens the writer's credibility by showing fairness to critics before the rebuttal.

options.text: suggest that the floodplain map was only partly accurate because its brown shading overstated the actual danger
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: 'Half' refers to half of the critics' charge, not to the map's accuracy; the passage never questions the data, only the color used to present it.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 3 and paragraph 4?

options.text: Paragraph 3 supplies an example that invites an objection, and paragraph 4 states that objection and answers it to sharpen the claim
options.label: correct
options.why: The floodplain story prompts the critics' charge of advocacy, which paragraph 4 raises, half concedes, and rebuts, arriving at the refined claim that she signed the argument.

options.text: Paragraph 3 offers one example of Quist's persuasive maps, and paragraph 4 adds a second example drawn from a different commission
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Paragraph 4 contains no new commission; it returns to the same pale blue floodplain to argue about advocacy.

options.text: Paragraph 3 praises Quist's boldness, and paragraph 4 retracts that praise by admitting her map distorted the county's data
options.label: reversal
options.why: Paragraph 4 concedes only that she had a position; it insists the data were sound and that the supposedly neutral map was equally advocated.

options.text: Paragraph 3 describes a local dispute, and paragraph 4 broadens it into a judgment about the ethics of all public officials
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Paragraph 4 stays within cartography, discussing whether any map lacks an advocate; it makes no claim about public officials generally.

items.stem: The writer develops paragraph 5 primarily by

options.text: describing a repeated process whose unvarying results exemplify the claim that a map's contents depend on its intended reader
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph lays out the exercise's steps (one dataset, three audiences, three maps), reports that the data never changed and the maps never matched, and draws the lesson about 'just the facts.'

options.text: contrasting Quist's teaching methods with the conventional training that apprentices received at other survey offices
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No other office or conventional training is mentioned in the paragraph; the only comparison is among the three maps themselves.

options.text: narrating the writer's own apprenticeship in chronological order from first lesson to final mastery of the craft
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The writer was among the apprentices, but the paragraph presents a single recurring exercise, not a chronological account of a career.

options.text: classifying every map into three fixed categories according to whether it serves families, companies, or children
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The three audiences are a teaching device illustrating variability, not a claim that maps fall into three permanent types.

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the colon in the sentence beginning "It struck me that she had kept it" is most effective because it

options.text: delays the explanation of "her finest map," so that the jar is redefined through the essay's governing idea of chosen omission
options.label: correct
options.why: The colon sets up the clause that explains the surprising phrase, tying the eraser crumbs to lines deliberately not let stand, which echoes the thesis about omission from paragraph 1.

options.text: introduces a list of the specific lines Quist erased over her forty-three years at the survey office
options.label: convention_error
options.why: What follows the colon is a single explanatory phrase, not a list, and no specific erased lines are named anywhere in the passage.

options.text: separates two independent claims, one about her habit of keeping the jar and another about her career, that are unrelated
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The second part directly explains the first; the colon marks dependence, not separation of unrelated ideas.

options.text: signals a turn toward sarcasm about the modesty of the jar compared with her publicly honored commissions
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The tone here is tender and elegiac; the writer sincerely elevates the jar rather than mocking it or the awards.

input.title: The Coffee Cans
paragraphs: Seed saving is a really important topic that a lot of people should know more about.
Every September, my grandmother Ilse dried bean pods on window screens in her garage and sorted the seeds into coffee cans labeled in pencil.
The beans were called Halloway Purples, and her family had carried them from farm to farm for four generations.
When she moved into assisted living two years ago, the cans came to me.
For most of human history, farmers saved seed from their best plants and replanted it the next spring.
During the twentieth century, many growers switched to F1 hybrids, which do not breed true.
Many old varieties disappeared.
I learned this from a pamphlet at the county extension office, and it made the coffee cans feel less like clutter and more like a responsibility.
Last spring I started a seed library in the back corner of the Harrow Creek Public Library, using a donated card catalog with sixty drawers.
Neighbors check out a packet, grow the plants, and return seed from the harvest in the fall.
Honestly, the first season was kind of a total disaster because half the borrowers never brought anything back.
I redesigned the return envelopes, added planting reminders by text message, and held a seed-cleaning night at the library in October.
This year, thirty-one of forty borrowers returned seed.
Saving seed has taught me that preserving something means sharing it, not locking it away.
I hope to keep doing this in college.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 15 with a closing sentence that links the seed library experience to a specific plan at Corliss College while echoing the lesson stated in sentence 14. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: At Corliss, I want to bring a drawer of Halloway Purples to the campus garden and find people willing to plant them and return the seed.
options.label: correct
options.why: Names a concrete Corliss plan and enacts the sharing-not-hoarding lesson of sentence 14.

options.text: Corliss College has a strong environmental studies program, which is one of the many reasons I am applying there this fall.
options.label: partially_right

options.text: Seed saving has a long history, and I believe more communities across the country should start seed libraries of their own.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Shifts to a general call to action and ignores the college context.

options.text: My grandmother still asks about the Halloway Purples every time I visit her, and I always tell her they are doing well.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: A touching detail, but it neither looks ahead to college nor restates the lesson.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 6 so that admissions readers who know little about gardening understand why hybrid seed could not be saved. Which revision best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: During the twentieth century, many growers began buying hybrid seed each year, because plants grown from saved hybrid seed often look nothing like their parents.
options.label: correct
options.why: Replaces jargon with a plain explanation of why saving hybrid seed fails.

options.text: During the twentieth century, many growers switched to F1 hybrids, a category of seed produced by crossing two distinct inbred parent lines.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Adds more technical detail but still never explains why the seed cannot be saved.

options.text: During the twentieth century, many growers foolishly switched to hybrid seed, abandoning centuries of careful work by their own ancestors.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Adds judgmental tone and still does not explain the problem with saving hybrids.

options.text: During the twentieth century, many growers switched to F1 hybrids, which do not breed true, as any experienced gardener already knows.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Assumes expert knowledge, alienating the very readers the writer wants to inform.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 1 with a thesis that makes a claim requiring support and previews the essay's movement from the grandmother's cans to seed-saving history to the seed library. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: My grandmother's coffee cans taught me that a seed survives only if someone keeps planting it, a lesson that led me into history and then to a library.
options.label: correct
options.why: States an arguable lesson and previews all three stages in order.

options.text: Heirloom seeds are disappearing all over the world, and saving them may be one of the most urgent challenges facing modern agriculture today.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Makes a sweeping global claim and previews none of the essay's personal structure.

options.text: My grandmother, Ilse, grew Halloway Purple beans in her garden for many decades and dried the seeds every September in her garage.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: A factual statement about the first paragraph only; no claim, no preview.

options.text: This essay will describe my grandmother's garage, the history of farming, and the seed library that I started at my town's public library.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Previews structure but announces topics without making any claim.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a transition at the beginning of sentence 7 that shows the loss of old varieties resulted from the change described in sentence 6. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: As a result, many old varieties disappeared.
options.label: correct
options.why: Signals cause and effect between the switch to hybrids and the loss.

options.text: Nevertheless, many old varieties disappeared.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals contrast where the relationship is causal.

options.text: Similarly, many old varieties disappeared.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals likeness, not consequence.

options.text: In the beginning, many old varieties disappeared.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Signals time sequence and obscures the causal link.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a transition at the beginning of sentence 12 that presents the changes as a direct response to the problem described in sentence 11. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: To fix this, I redesigned the return envelopes,
options.label: correct
options.why: Directly ties the changes to the low return rate in sentence 11.

options.text: For example, I redesigned the return envelopes,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Presents the changes as an illustration of the failure rather than a response.

options.text: Even so, I redesigned the return envelopes,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Implies the changes happened despite the problem, not because of it.

options.text: Before that, I redesigned the return envelopes,
options.label: reversal
options.why: Places the fixes before the failure, reversing the sequence.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 11 so that it reports the setback in the candid but composed tone suited to an admissions committee. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The first season, however, fell short: half the borrowers never returned any seed.
options.label: correct
options.why: Honest about failure while keeping a measured, mature register.

options.text: The first season, sadly, was a catastrophe, since half the borrowers just bailed.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Melodramatic and slangy; still too casual.

options.text: The first season was perfectly fine, though some borrowers forgot to return seed.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Misrepresents the setback and undercuts the later improvement.

options.text: The first season, though, totally flopped, because half the borrowers ghosted me.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Retains informal slang inappropriate for admissions readers.

input.title: Testimony on Ordinance 14-B
paragraphs: Good evening, members of the Larkhaven City Council.
My name is Odile Strand, and I have lived on Quarry Hill Road for twenty-two years.
Tonight I want to talk about lights.
Every second Saturday, the Larkhaven Stargazers Club sets up telescopes in the gravel lot behind the public library.
Ten years ago, we could show visitors the faint smudge of the Andromeda galaxy without much trouble.
Since the city installed the new white LED globes along Cutler Avenue, that smudge has disappeared from our lot entirely.
Last spring a nine-year-old girl looked through my eyepiece, saw only a gray haze, and asked whether the telescope was broken.
The problem is not that the lights are on but where they point.
The Cutler Avenue fixtures are uncovered globes that throw about a third of their light sideways and upward, where it lights nothing but the sky.
The town of Fenwick Ridge, forty miles north, replaced its globes with fully shielded fixtures and reported that its electricity bill for street lighting dropped by 18 percent.
Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, they cost about the same as the globes the city currently uses and they also last just as long as the globes do.
Anyway, that is basically all I have got, so thanks for listening to me ramble.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 12 with a conclusion that suits a formal hearing, asks the council for a specific action on the ordinance, and returns to an image from earlier in the testimony. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: I urge you to require shielded fixtures in Ordinance 14-B, so that the next child at our eyepiece sees a galaxy instead of a haze.
options.label: correct
options.why: Formal, makes a specific request about the ordinance, and echoes the girl's gray haze from sentence 7.

options.text: Astronomy has given me decades of joy, and I hope that more residents of Larkhaven will join our club on Saturdays.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Promotes the club rather than requesting any action on the ordinance.

options.text: Honestly, those Cutler Avenue globes are a total eyesore, and you folks should rip every one of them out tomorrow.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Too casual and combative for council testimony, and it ignores the earlier image.

options.text: Thank you for your time this evening, and I would be happy to answer any questions the council may have for me.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Appropriately formal, but makes no request and recalls nothing from the testimony.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 2 that tells the council why she is speaking by linking her introduction to the agenda item under discussion. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: I am here as a member of the Larkhaven Stargazers Club to speak on Ordinance 14-B, the streetlight replacement plan.
options.label: correct
options.why: Names her role and the specific agenda item, so the introduction leads into the testimony.

options.text: Quarry Hill Road is a quiet street, and in summer my neighbors often sit outside on their porches after dinner.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Adds neighborhood detail but never mentions the ordinance or why she is testifying.

options.text: Before I retired, I worked as a pharmacist at a small drugstore on the east side of town for many years.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Gives personal background that has nothing to do with lighting or the agenda item.

options.text: Many cities around the world are now debating how much artificial light their residents actually need at night.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Talks about a global debate instead of the specific local agenda item.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 3 into a thesis that takes a position needing proof and previews both the problem and the solution she discusses later. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: I will argue that unshielded streetlights are erasing our night sky and that shielded fixtures could restore it at no added cost.
options.label: correct
options.why: Takes an arguable position and previews both the problem (paragraph 2) and the solution (paragraph 3).

options.text: Tonight I want to share my lifelong love of astronomy, a hobby I have enjoyed ever since I was a child.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Personal and not arguable; it previews neither the lighting problem nor the solution.

options.text: Light pollution is a growing problem facing many towns and cities across the country in recent decades.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: A general observation that previews none of the draft's specific argument.

options.text: I will ask the council to ban all outdoor lighting in Larkhaven after midnight in order to protect the sky.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Proposes a ban that the draft never argues for; the draft calls for shielding, not darkness.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that explains how the girl's experience supports her claim that the new lighting has hidden the night sky. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The telescope was working fine; what she saw was the glow of Cutler Avenue covering a sky our children once shared.
options.label: correct
options.why: Turns the anecdote into evidence by blaming the haze on the streetlights, which supports the claim.

options.text: Telescopes like mine can cost several hundred dollars, so her worry that it was broken was a fair one.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Comments on what the equipment costs instead of connecting the haze to the lighting.

options.text: I explained to her that the Andromeda galaxy is roughly two and a half million light-years from Earth.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Adds a fact about astronomy but does not explain how the anecdote supports the claim about the lights.

options.text: She was easily the most curious child who has visited our club at any point in the last decade.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Praises the girl with no support and has no link to the argument about lighting.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 that explains how the Fenwick Ridge example supports her argument, building on the point in sentence 9 about wasted light. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Because shielded fixtures stop sending light into the sky, a town pays only for light that actually reaches its streets.
options.label: correct
options.why: Uses the wasted light from sentence 9 to explain why shielding reduced Fenwick Ridge's bill.

options.text: Fenwick Ridge is also known for its fall apple festival, which draws visitors from all across the region.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: An irrelevant detail about the town that explains nothing about the evidence.

options.text: This proves that every city in the state would save exactly 18 percent by switching to shielded fixtures.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Overgeneralizes one town's result instead of explaining it.

options.text: Fenwick Ridge, like Larkhaven, is full of residents who care deeply about their community and its future.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Claims the towns are alike but does not connect the savings to shielding or wasted light.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 11 so that it is concise and grammatically correct while keeping both of its claims about cost and durability. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, cost about the same as the city's current globes and last just as long.
options.label: correct
options.why: Drops the doubled subject and repeated words but keeps both claims.

options.text: Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, they cost about the same as the city's globes and last as long.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Keeps the extra subject pronoun 'they,' which is ungrammatical.

options.text: Shielded fixtures, which aim light down toward the street below, are similar in cost to the globes the city uses now and are also similar in how long they last.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Grammatically correct but still wordy and repetitive.

options.text: Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, cost somewhat more than the city's current globes but last much longer.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Changes both claims and weakens the writer's point that switching costs nothing extra.

blueprint.speaker: Dolores Keach, a licensed master plumber who runs a small shop and writes the recurring column 'From the Crawlspace' for her regional trade association's newsletter; she speaks as someone who has been both an apprentice and, recently, a mentor.
blueprint.audience: Fellow members of the Harrow County Mechanical Contractors Association: working plumbers, shop owners, retired members and apprentices who will vote at the next meeting.
blueprint.exigence: A board memo proposing to end the association's ride-along mentorship program (first-year apprentices paired with retired members two days a month) and replace it with a library of professionally produced training videos, with a vote scheduled for the following month.
blueprint.purpose: To persuade members to reject the proposal and keep the ride-along program by showing that what it transmits cannot be recorded, and to urge them to attend the meeting and question the board's cost figures.
blueprint.context: A quarterly column in a trade association newsletter; the writer assumes readers share trade vocabulary (sweating copper, backflow code, slab leak, listening rod) and a stake in apprentice training.
blueprint.claim: The ride-along program should be preserved because the kind of knowledge it transmits, a habit of noticing passed through hours of shared attention, cannot be captured in recorded instruction; its apparent inefficiency is its purpose.
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: P1 states the occasion (the memo) and the position (videos would be a mistake). P2 narrates the writer's own apprenticeship with Augie Pell to show how noticing is taught through time and touch. P3 generalizes the anecdote into a distinction between recordable procedural knowledge and the unrecordable habit of noticing. P4 concedes the board's arithmetic (cost, limited reach, stubborn elders) and then rebuts by redefining the expense of hours as the program's whole point. P5 shifts to a confession: the writer, as elder, learned from a young apprentice, so the program also updates the retired members. P6 closes with a direct call to attend the meeting and ask what the cost figure fails to count.
evidence_types: personal anecdote (two ride-alongs, as apprentice and as elder)
concrete trade examples (hum in a pipe, flux smell, thermal image)
approximate program figures conceded from the board's memo
definition and distinction between two kinds of knowledge

devices.function: Narrates the writer's apprenticeship with Augie Pell to show how the habit of noticing is transmitted through hours of shared attention rather than demonstration.
The three-word 'I heard nothing.' after a long descriptive sentence dramatizes the apprentice's blankness before the lesson.
Colons introduce the explanation of the hum, the catalog of things a plumber notices, and the admission that mentoring runs both ways.
Hum leads to loose strap leads to worn pipe, showing the practical stakes of noticing.
Distinguishes recordable procedural knowledge from the unrecordable 'habit of noticing' that defines a plumber.
'a plumber' versus 'someone who owns plumbing tools' sharpens the distinction between skill and equipment.
'No camera records a habit.' lands as a blunt verdict after the long catalog of noticed details.
Attention 'shapes' attention; time is a 'medium'; mentoring is 'traffic' that runs both ways, all framing mentorship as a physical transfer.
Grants the board's arithmetic and the elders' stubbornness, then rebuts by redefining expense as the program's point.
Approximate cost and reach figures, offered as the board's own case, establish fairness before rebuttal.
'to put it gently, set in their ways' concedes the elders' difficulty with wry restraint.
Three parallel verbs give the video library's advantages a brisk fairness; the three 'and then' clauses in 26 trace the writer's change of heart.
'not made the program efficient; you have removed the thing it was for' and 'not a flaw / a description' set the board's framing against the writer's.
Moves from firm rebuttal to candid, self-deprecating confession, which prepares the reversal that mentoring runs both ways.
The Teo Marsh ride-along shows the elder learning from the apprentice, extending the program's value.
'carried a tablet the way I carry a pipe wrench' equates the apprentice's tool with the writer's, signaling parity of expertise.
The young apprentice's patience, contrasted with Augie's, wryly reverses the expected generational roles.
The writer's experience on both sides of the ride-along grounds her authority to judge the program.
Imperatives and second person turn the column into a call to action for the meeting.

tone_shifts.from: firm, argumentative rebuttal of the board

blueprint.counterargument: The board's position (sentences 17 through 19): the program is expensive, reaches only about thirty apprentices, depends on retired members who can be stubborn or dismissive, while a video library would cost less, reach everyone, and spare apprentices the elders' condescension. The writer grants all of this and then argues that the hours are the point, since attention can only be passed through time, and that the elders themselves are being updated by the program.

input.title: What the Spreadsheet Cannot Hear
paragraphs: The memo arrived on a Tuesday, between a boiler quote and a reminder that my van inspection was overdue.
The board, it said, is considering ending the ride-along program, which pairs first-year apprentices with a retired member for two days a month, and replacing it with a library of training videos.
The videos, the memo assured us, would be professionally produced.
I have no doubt that they would be.
I also have no doubt that they would be a mistake, and I would like to explain why before the vote next month.
When I was nineteen I rode along with Augie Pell, who had been sweating copper since before I was born and who did not, as far as I could tell, approve of me.
On my third day he stopped in a basement in Fenwick Heights, laid his palm against a supply line, and asked me what I heard.
I heard nothing.
He said that was the problem: the line was humming, faintly, and the hum meant a loose strap upstream that would, in a year or two, wear a hole through the pipe.
He did not show me where the strap was; he made me stand there with my own hand on the pipe until I could feel what he felt, which took most of the afternoon and all of my pride.
There is a kind of knowledge that can be written down, and the trades are full of it: clearances, torque values, the order in which you open valves.
A video carries that knowledge perfectly well.
But there is another kind of knowledge that lives only in a person, and it is the kind that separates a plumber from someone who owns plumbing tools.
It is the habit of noticing: the faint hum, the smell of flux mixed wrong, the way a homeowner's voice changes when the leak she describes is not the one she is worried about.
No camera records a habit.
A habit is transferred the way Augie transferred it, by standing next to someone long enough that his attention starts to shape yours.
I will grant the board its arithmetic.
The program costs roughly 40,000 dollars a year, it reaches perhaps thirty apprentices, and some of our retired members are, to put it gently, set in their ways.
A video library would cost less, reach everyone, and never tell an apprentice that her generation does not know how to work.
But the expense that looks like waste on the spreadsheet is the whole point.
What we are paying for is hours in basements, because time is the only medium in which attention passes from one pair of hands to another.
Cut the hours and you have not made the program efficient; you have removed the thing it was for.
I should admit something the memo does not mention: the traffic on those ride-alongs does not run in one direction.
Last spring I rode along myself, as the elder this time, with Teo Marsh, twenty-two, who carried a tablet the way I carry a pipe wrench.
On our second job he pulled up a thermal image of a wall and found, in four minutes, a slab leak I had planned to hunt all morning with a listening rod.
I was annoyed, and then I was grateful, and then I asked him to show me how the thing worked.
He was patient with me, which is more than I can say for Augie.
The retired members are not only being preserved by this program; they are being updated.
So here is what I am asking.

Come to the meeting on the fourteenth, and when the board presents its cost per apprentice, ask whether the number counts the pipes that did not burst or the old plumbers who learned to read a thermal camera.
You will not get an answer; nobody has one.
That is not a flaw in the program.
It is a description of what it does.

items.stem: The passage is most directly a response to which of the following situations?

options.text: A proposal under consideration by the writer's association to replace a mentorship program with recorded training materials ahead of a scheduled vote
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 1 identifies the board memo proposing to end the ride-along program in favor of training videos and the writer's intent to argue against it 'before the vote next month.'

options.text: A disagreement between the writer and her former mentor about whether new diagnostic tools belong in the hands of first-year apprentices
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Augie and the thermal camera appear as illustrations within the argument; no dispute with Augie about tools is described, and the occasion is the board memo.

options.text: A shortage of retired members willing to volunteer their time, which has left most apprentices without an assigned mentor for the coming year
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage never mentions a shortage of volunteers; the retired members are described as present, if 'set in their ways.'

options.text: A request from apprentices that the association deliver its training through video so that they can learn at their own pace
options.label: reversal
options.why: The proposal comes from the board, not the apprentices, and the writer presents apprentices as beneficiaries of the program rather than as advocates for its replacement.

items.stem: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.text: Retired tradespeople gain as much from the ride-along program as the apprentices do, so the association owes it to its elders to continue it
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The two-way benefit in paragraph 5 is a supporting extension of the argument, introduced as 'something the memo does not mention,' not the thesis announced in paragraph 1 and developed in paragraphs 3 and 4.

options.text: The ride-along program should be kept because the knowledge it passes on cannot be captured by recorded instruction
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 1 states the position (videos 'would be a mistake'), paragraph 3 explains that the habit of noticing is a knowledge 'no camera records,' and paragraph 4 argues the hours are 'the whole point.'

options.text: Training videos are useless for teaching the trades because the skills involved can only ever be learned through physical practice
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The writer explicitly concedes that a video 'carries that knowledge perfectly well' for written-down matters like torque values, so the passage does not claim videos are useless.

options.text: The program's cost is justified because the burst pipes and callbacks it prevents would cost the association far more than the stipends
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The closing paragraph says the benefits cannot be counted and that 'nobody has' such a number; the writer declines to make a cost-benefit case and instead argues the expense is the point.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the writer's acknowledgment that the program 'reaches perhaps thirty apprentices' and that some retired members are 'set in their ways' primarily serves to

options.text: show that she has weighed the board's practical objections fairly before redefining the program's expense as its purpose
options.label: correct
options.why: 'I will grant the board its arithmetic' opens a concession that lists cost, reach and stubborn elders, and the 'But' in the following sentence turns the conceded expense into 'the whole point.'

options.text: signal her reluctant agreement that a video library would ultimately serve first-year apprentices better than the elders do
options.label: reversal
options.why: The concession is immediately rebutted; the writer argues that cutting hours removes 'the thing it was for,' so she does not agree that videos would serve apprentices better.

options.text: introduce evidence that the program should be expanded so that it can reach every apprentice rather than only thirty
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The figure of thirty is granted as a limitation the board cites, not offered as grounds for expansion; the writer never proposes enlarging the program.

options.text: undermine the board's cost figures by exposing the benefits that its spreadsheet fails to count
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The uncounted benefits appear in paragraph 6, not here; in paragraph 4 the writer accepts the arithmetic rather than disputing it.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 2 and paragraph 3?

options.text: Paragraph 3 qualifies paragraph 2 by conceding that the writer's experience with one mentor may not represent the program as a whole
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Paragraph 3 contains no such concession; it treats the Augie episode as the model of how a habit 'is transferred' rather than as a possibly unrepresentative case.

options.text: Paragraph 3 draws a general distinction between two kinds of knowledge out of the specific lesson narrated in paragraph 2
options.label: correct
options.why: The basement scene (the hum, the hand on the pipe) becomes in paragraph 3 the example of a 'habit of noticing' that 'no camera records,' and the paragraph ends by returning to 'the way Augie transferred it.'

options.text: Paragraph 3 refutes the harsh method of instruction described in paragraph 2 by proposing a gentler way to teach attentiveness
options.label: reversal
options.why: Far from refuting Augie's method, paragraph 3 endorses it as the only way a habit is transferred, 'by standing next to someone long enough.'

options.text: Paragraph 3 turns to a different subject, the value of videos for code updates, leaving paragraph 2 as personal background
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The remark that a video carries written-down knowledge is a brief concession within the distinction, not a new subject; the paragraph's weight falls on the knowledge that lives only in a person.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes how paragraph 5 contributes to the writer's line of reasoning?

options.text: It extends the argument by showing that the program also benefits the retired members, adding a value a video library could not replace
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph opens by admitting 'the traffic on those ride-alongs does not run in one direction' and closes with the elders being 'updated,' a second benefit that depends on shared hours rather than recordings.

options.text: It weakens the argument by admitting that new technology can find a leak faster than the habits of noticing celebrated in paragraph 3
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The thermal camera anecdote is framed as evidence for the program, since the elder learned the tool through a ride-along; the writer presents it as support, not as a damaging admission.

options.text: It restates the concession of paragraph 4 in personal terms to show that the writer shares the board's doubts about stubborn elders
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Although the writer admits annoyance, the paragraph does not reiterate the board's objections; it introduces a benefit 'the memo does not mention.'

options.text: It establishes the writer's own competence with thermal imaging in order to recommend the equipment to the newsletter's readers
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The writer describes learning the tool from Teo, but the point is that the program taught her, not that readers should buy thermal cameras.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the semicolon in the sentence 'Cut the hours and you have not made the program efficient; you have removed the thing it was for' primarily serves to

options.text: balance the board's intended result against the actual result in two matched clauses, so the correction lands as a verdict
options.label: correct
options.why: The semicolon joins two parallel 'you have' clauses without a conjunction, setting 'not made the program efficient' directly against 'removed the thing it was for' and giving the second clause the force of a judgment.

options.text: introduce a list of the program's purposes that the board's memo has overlooked in its calculation of cost
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: No list follows the semicolon; it is a single clause, and the uncounted benefits appear in paragraph 6, not here.

options.text: mark a pause that softens the writer's criticism of the board by separating it from the sharper claim that follows
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The tight pairing of clauses intensifies rather than softens; the writer has just insisted the expense is 'the whole point' and uses the semicolon to deliver the blunt consequence.

options.text: present the second clause as a tentative afterthought that the writer adds in case the first clause seems too strong
options.label: reversal
options.why: The second clause is the stronger and more definite of the two, stating what has actually happened; nothing in its wording is tentative.

input.title: What the Shoreline Taught Us: A Report on Merrow Point's Retreating Coast
paragraphs: The ocean has always been a powerful force in human history.
This fall, our environmental science class spent nine weeks measuring the bluffs along Gannet Road.
We used survey stakes, old aerial photographs from the town library, and interviews with eleven residents.
What we found out and discovered in the end was that the bluff edge has moved back an average of about two feet every single year since 1990.
The town's first answer to erosion was the concrete seawall built below Pell Street in 1998.
The wall protected the houses directly behind it for many years.
Anyone who still thinks walls are the answer simply has not looked at the beach.
Waves bouncing off the concrete have scoured away the sand in front of it, and the beach at Pell Street has nearly vanished.
Dune restoration is a better way to protect the coast.
Last spring, volunteers planted beach grass and set sand fences along the north end of Little Cove.
Our stake measurements there showed that the bluff lost less than four inches this year, compared with two feet near the seawall.
The town has also moved the Gannet Road pump station 200 feet inland, and the lifeguard tower now sits on movable skids.
Moving buildings is expensive.
Rebuilding them after a storm costs more.
Our class recommends that the council fund more dune planting and begin planning which structures should move first.

options.label: correct

options.text: Coastal towns all over the world have been fighting erosion for centuries, often using whatever materials were close at hand.

options.label: too_narrow

items.stem: Many panel members own shorefront homes and supported the seawall. The writer wants to revise sentence 7 so it acknowledges their view respectfully while still pointing to the wall's drawback. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The wall made sense when it was built, but its effect on the beach in front of it deserves a closer look.
options.label: correct

options.text: Supporters of the wall were frankly shortsighted, though they probably meant well at the time.
options.label: wrong_tone

options.text: The wall has been a complete success, and nobody could reasonably question its value to the town.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Drops the drawback and contradicts sentence 8.

options.label: wrong_function

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 9 that offers evidence supporting the claim that dune restoration specifically protects the coast. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: At the town's older restored dune near Hollis Beach, our stakes showed almost no bluff loss over three years of storms.
options.label: correct
options.why: Gives measured evidence linking dunes directly to reduced erosion.

options.text: Beach grass is a hardy plant that can grow in salty, sandy soil where few other plants survive.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Describes the plant but offers no evidence that dunes protect the coast.

options.text: Several residents we interviewed said they find the dunes prettier than the gray concrete of the wall.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Shows preference about appearance, not proof of protection.

options.text: Erosion is a problem that affects shorelines on every continent and costs governments large sums.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Addresses erosion generally, not the effectiveness of dunes.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 11 that explains how the measurements support the paragraph's claim about dune restoration. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: That difference suggests the dunes absorb wave energy that the wall only redirects onto the sand below it.
options.label: correct
options.why: Interprets the numbers and connects them to why dunes outperform the wall.

options.text: We took these measurements each month using the same stakes, so the numbers are consistent from season to season.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Describes method rather than explaining what the evidence means for the claim.

options.text: Four inches is about the length of a smartphone, while two feet is roughly the length of a bike wheel.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Makes the numbers vivid but never links them to the claim about dunes.

options.text: This proves that dunes will stop erosion permanently on every stretch of Merrow Point's shoreline.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Overstates one year's data at one site into a sweeping guarantee.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 4 to eliminate redundancy while keeping its meaning. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: We found that the bluff edge has retreated an average of about two feet a year since 1990.
options.label: correct
options.why: Removes the repeated 'found out and discovered' and 'every single' while keeping all facts.

options.text: What we found, and what we discovered, was that the bluff edge moved about two feet a year since 1990.
options.label: convention_error

options.text: We found that the bluff edge has retreated quite a bit over the years since the early nineties.

items.stem: The writer wants to combine sentences 13 and 14 into one sentence that shows the cost of moving buildings is outweighed by the cost of rebuilding them. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.label: correct

options.text: Moving buildings is expensive, so rebuilding them after a storm costs more.
options.label: illogical_relationship

options.text: Moving buildings is expensive, rebuilding them after a storm costs more.
options.label: convention_error

options.text: Because rebuilding costs more after a storm, moving buildings is expensive.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Turns the relationship around into a false cause.

P1:
1. Behind the Brambleton subdivision, past the last cul-de-sac, there is a flat field of cattails and broken drainage pipe that most of us have never noticed.
2. Forty years ago it was Cutler's Marsh, until a developer dug ditches to dry it out for houses that were never built.
3. Wetlands are important for many reasons.
P2:
4. This spring the Larkfield town council will vote on whether to spend 180,000 dollars to fill the ditches and let the marsh flood again.
5. Restoring the marsh would definitely end flooding in Brambleton forever.
6. Last April, after two days of rain, water reached the doorsteps on Finch Lane, and the town paid 64,000 dollars to pump basements.
7. A marsh works like a sponge, soaking up runoff and releasing it slowly.
P3:
8. Some residents worry that standing water will bring mosquitoes.
9. The town's own consultant, Dr. Ilse Varga of the fictional Pell Valley Institute... just "a consultant hired by the town, ecologist Ilse Varga, reported that a healthy marsh draws dragonflies and frogs that eat mosquito larvae."
P4:
10. Our biology classes could use the marsh as an outdoor lab, measuring water quality instead of reading about it.
11. Anyway, the council should totally go for it, because it's a no-brainer.

Q1 intro thesis-ish end of para 1), 11 closing (Q2 conclusion), 5 overstated (4.C), between 8 and 9 transition missing (6.B: "However," vs need contrast — sentence 9 opener), 6.C: add after 7 an analogy/comparison? Q5: add example supporting cost comparison? Let's do 6.C: writer wants to add a comparison showing restoration cost is reasonable — sentence after 6: "Three floods like last April's would cost the town more than the entire restoration." Distractors. 8.A: sentence 11 tone? that's Q2 conclusion. Make 8.A on sentence 10 phrase? Better: put tone issue in sentence 8: "Some residents freak out that..." -> respectful. Change 8 to "Some residents freak out about mosquitoes." Then transition Q on sentence 9 start. Fine.

input.title: Let Cutler's Marsh Flood Again
paragraphs: Behind the Brambleton subdivision, past the last cul-de-sac, lies a flat field of cattails and cracked drainage pipe that most of us have never noticed.
Forty years ago it was Cutler's Marsh, until a developer dug ditches to dry it out for houses that were never built.
Wetlands are important for many reasons.
This spring the Larkfield town council will vote on whether to spend 180,000 dollars to fill those ditches and let the marsh hold water again.
Restoring the marsh would definitely end flooding in Brambleton forever.
Last April, after two days of rain, water reached the doorsteps on Finch Lane, and the town paid 64,000 dollars to pump out basements.
A marsh works like a sponge, soaking up runoff and releasing it slowly.
Some residents totally freak out about mosquitoes.
An ecologist hired by the town, Ilse Varga, reported that a healthy marsh draws dragonflies and frogs that eat mosquito larvae.
Our biology classes could use the marsh as an outdoor lab, measuring water quality instead of just reading about it.
Anyway, the council should totally go for it, because it's a no-brainer.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 3 with a sentence that ends the introduction by stating the editorial's specific position on the council's upcoming vote. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The council should vote to restore Cutler's Marsh, which would ease flooding, curb mosquitoes and teach students.
options.label: correct
options.why: States a clear, arguable position on the vote and previews the three reasons the draft develops.

options.text: Wetlands around the world filter water, shelter birds and store carbon in ways scientists still study.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Talks about wetlands in general and takes no position on Larkfield's vote.

options.text: The developer who drained the marsh decades ago should never have been allowed to dig those ditches.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Argues about past events, not the restoration vote the editorial addresses.

options.text: Whether the marsh should be restored is a question that each reader will have to decide alone.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Avoids taking any position, defeating the persuasive purpose.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 11 with a conclusion that suits a school newspaper audience and urges readers to take a specific action before the vote. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Before the spring vote, ask your parents to write the council and support bringing Cutler's Marsh back.
options.label: correct
options.why: Uses an appropriate tone and gives readers a concrete action tied to the vote.

options.text: Cutler's Marsh has quite a history, and it will be interesting to watch what the council finally decides.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Observes rather than urging any action.

options.text: Seriously, anyone who votes against the marsh plan is clueless and should just stay home this spring.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Insulting and slangy, unfit for a respectful editorial.

options.text: Our biology teachers already have lab equipment, so outdoor water testing would cost the school nothing.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Adds a new unsupported claim rather than concluding with a call to action.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 5 so that the claim about flooding is qualified to match the evidence in sentences 6 and 7. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Restoring the marsh would likely reduce the flooding that Brambleton suffers after heavy rains.
options.label: correct

options.text: Restoring the marsh would certainly stop all flooding in Brambleton and the rest of Larkfield.

options.text: Restoring the marsh might, some say, perhaps help with water in a few places now and then.

options.why: Qualifies the claim but hedges so heavily that it no longer makes a useful point.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 9 (adjusting capitalization as needed) to show that Varga's finding challenges the concern in sentence 8. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: However,
options.label: correct
options.why: Signals contrast between the worry and the evidence that answers it.

options.text: Similarly,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals likeness, but the finding opposes the worry.

options.text: As a result,
options.label: illogical_relationship

options.text: For instance,

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that uses a comparison to show the restoration cost is reasonable. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Neighboring Ashby spent far more on a new soccer complex that few residents ever use.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Compares to an unrelated project that says nothing about flood savings.

options.text: Pumping basements is expensive, and many families also paid to replace their furnaces.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Mentions costs but never measures them against the restoration price.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 8 so that it presents residents' concern respectfully, in a tone suited to a newspaper read by parents and teachers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Some residents are understandably worried that standing water will bring mosquitoes.
options.label: correct
options.why: Respectful, measured wording that sets up the rebuttal fairly.

options.text: Some residents are freaking out big time about a bunch of mosquitoes.

input.title: What Your Phone Doesn't Know About Our Clay
paragraphs: Every Saturday at the Hollins Lane Community Garden, someone asks why their tomatoes split, and every Saturday someone else answers by holding up a phone.
I am Ruth Okafor-Lind, I tend plot 14, and I want to make a case for a building most of us drive right past: the Pell Street Branch Library.
Libraries are good things to have in a town.
A search engine gives you answers in a hurry, but it does not know our soil.
Our clay holds water for days, and advice written for sandy coastal gardens can drown a seedling here.
Pell Street keeps local knowledge that no search result can match.

Last spring I asked a librarian there, Mr. Dowd, about blossom-end rot, and he pulled out a county pamphlet from 1987 and a binder of notes left by a gardener who worked this same lot forty years ago.
Search engines are completely useless for gardeners and should never be trusted.
Last year, the branch also began lending seeds from an old wooden card catalog near the front desk.
Gardeners borrow a packet in April, and in the fall they return seeds saved from their strongest plants.
The reason why this is important is because of the fact that the seeds that come back each year are seeds that have already proven that they can survive in our clay and our short summers.
The county board votes on the library's budget on March 9.
Board members have proposed cutting the branch's Saturday hours, the only hours many working gardeners can visit, and the plan would close it's seed desk on weekends.
If you have ever borrowed a seed packet, a book, or a librarian's patience, come to the meeting and say so.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 3 so that it states her position in terms that appeal to her audience of practical gardeners who usually turn to their phones for advice. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: For gardeners who care about what actually grows in this clay, the library offers local know-how and free seeds that a phone cannot.
options.label: correct
options.why: Speaks to the gardeners' practical concern (results in local soil) and previews the library's concrete benefits.

options.text: Libraries remain essential institutions for cultivating information literacy in a democratic, digitally saturated society.

Draft plan: a museum exhibit essay for a fictional county historical society exhibit of letters. Writer: a volunteer docent.

Sentences:
P1:
1 When the Harrow Creek Historical Society opened its new gallery of family letters this spring, visitors kept stopping at one display case.
2 Inside is a letter from 1911, written by a fourteen-year-old named Ada Pruitt to her brother working the grain barges downriver.
3 Many younger visitors told our docents they could not read a single word of it.
4 Cursive is important in many ways. (vague thesis — 4.B)
P2:
5 The most obvious reason to teach cursive is access to the past.
6 Our archive holds more than 3,000 handwritten documents, from ledgers to wedding invitations.
7 A student who cannot read script must rely on someone else's transcription, and transcriptions leave things out. (6.A commentary missing after)
8 In Ada's letter, for example, she crossed out "lonesome" and wrote "busy" above it.
P3:
9 Cursive also helps students learn.
10 Teachers at the Lindell Street School reported that their students enjoyed the new handwriting unit. (weak evidence — 4.A)
11 Anyone who thinks cursive is useless is honestly just being kind of lazy about history. (tone — 8.A / 2.B audience: families, skeptics)
P4:
12 We do not argue that cursive should replace keyboarding.
13 We think that schools should set aside some time, perhaps a few weeks, for the purpose of teaching students how to read and also how to write cursive script, which is a skill that is valuable. (wordy — 8.B)
14 Ada's letter is waiting for them.

Questions:
2.B: sentence 11 revised for audience of parents skeptical. Distinct from 8.A? 8.A could target sentence 11 too; better to make 8.A target different word. Let 2.B add a sentence after 12 acknowledging parents' concern about crowded school days. 8.A: sentence 11 replace for respectful tone.

input.title: Ada's Letter
paragraphs: When the Harrow Creek Historical Society opened its new gallery of family letters this spring, visitors kept stopping at one display case.
Inside is a letter from 1911, written by a fourteen-year-old named Ada Pruitt to her brother, who was working the grain barges downriver.
Many younger visitors told our docents they could not read a single word of it.
Cursive is important in many ways.
The most obvious reason to teach cursive is access to the past.
Our archive holds more than 3,000 handwritten documents, from feed-store ledgers to wedding invitations.
A student who cannot read script must rely on someone else's transcription, and transcriptions leave things out.
In Ada's letter, for example, she crossed out the word lonesome and wrote busy above it.
Cursive also helps students learn.
Teachers at the Lindell Street School reported that their students enjoyed the new handwriting unit.
Anyone who thinks cursive is useless is honestly just being kind of lazy about history.
We do not argue that cursive should replace keyboarding.
We think that schools should set aside some time, perhaps a few weeks, for the purpose of teaching students how to read and also how to write cursive script, which is a skill that is valuable.
Ada's letter is waiting for them.

options.label: correct

input.title: Why Our Brains Miss the First Bell
paragraphs: Every weekday at 6:05 a.m., my alarm goes off in a house where everyone else is still asleep.
By the time the first bell rings at 7:20, I have been awake for over an hour, but my brain has not caught up.
Sleep is an important topic that affects many people in different ways.
Scientists who study sleep describe a shift that happens during puberty.
The body's internal clock moves later, so teenagers often do not feel sleepy until around 11 p.m.
An alarm at 6 a.m. therefore cuts the night short no matter how disciplined a student is.
Teens also need more sleep than adults, roughly eight to ten hours a night.
In October, our club decided to test this locally, and twelve members kept sleep logs for two weeks.
On school nights, the average was six hours and ten minutes.
On weekends, the same students slept almost nine hours.
That gap suggests that we are not lazy; we are just totally wrecked by a schedule that ignores biology.
Some people worry that a later start would mess up bus routes and after-school sports.
Those concerns are real.
Districts that have shifted their schedules have found ways to stagger buses and adjust practice times.
The school board votes on the 8:30 proposal on November 18.
Anyway, that is pretty much what I think about sleep.

options.label: correct
options.why: Names a concrete action tied to the vote date in sentence 16, which the newsletter's readers can take.

options.text: Sleep science keeps changing, so maybe in a few years everyone will finally agree on the best start time.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Defers the issue rather than calling readers to act before the vote.

options.text: In the end, getting enough sleep is up to each of us, whatever time the first bell happens to ring.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Puts the burden back on individuals and undercuts the draft's argument that the schedule is the problem.

options.label: partially_right
options.why: Repeats data from paragraph 3 but asks readers to do nothing.

options.text: Bedtimes in the logs barely changed, with most members asleep around 11:15 either way, so the gap came from wake-up times.
options.label: correct
options.why: Shows bedtimes held steady, so the difference must come from the early alarm. That supports sentence 12.

options.text: Several members said they drank coffee or energy drinks on school mornings to stay alert in first period.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Shows students are tired but says nothing about whether bedtimes or wake times caused it.

options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Deals with the effects of lost sleep, not its cause.

options.text: Many members admitted to staying up late scrolling on their phones, often well past midnight.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Points to late bedtimes, which contradicts the claim it is supposed to support.

options.label: partially_right
options.why: Takes a position but previews none of the evidence and rests on a vague assertion.

options.text: Teenagers' body clocks shift later during puberty, and our club spent two weeks logging the sleep of twelve members.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Summarizes the content but takes no position on the proposal.

options.label: too_broad
options.why: Stays neutral and general, so there is nothing to prove and no structure is previewed.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 15 (adjusting capitalization as needed) to signal a shift from granting the concern in sentence 14 to answering it. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

input.title: A Proposal for Whistle Week
paragraphs: Last month at the Harlow Ridge rec fields, I watched a fourteen-year-old referee named Milo Brandt stop an under-10 soccer game because a parent would not stop yelling at him.
Milo finished the game, but he turned in his whistle the next week.
Sports officials are important.
The Ridge County Youth League reports that it lost 23 of its 61 teen referees last season.
Many of those officials are students at our school.
Without referees, games get canceled, and younger kids lose the chance to play.
Officials who quit often name one reason: the way adults and fans treat them.
I am proposing that the council sponsor a Whistle Week in March.
Students who play sports would spend one practice officiating a scrimmage instead of playing in it.
We would also post signs at home games reminding fans that many referees are teenagers.
This is a super cheap fix that would totally work.
The signs would cost about 140 dollars, and the league has offered to lend us flags and whistles.
Some people think yelling at referees is just part of sports.
Fans who have worn the stripes themselves tend to yell less.
Whistle Week is a way to teach respect.
It is a way that would help keep referees like Milo, and it would help them stay in officiating.

input.title: What We Heard When We Reopened
paragraphs: When the Linden Street Branch reopened in March, the first thing many patrons noticed was not the new skylights but the sound.
Noise is a big problem in lots of places these days.

Between the delivery trucks idling on Corwin Avenue and the leaf blowers that circle the plaza every Tuesday, our reading room now averages 68 decibels by midafternoon, according to a meter our staff borrowed from the county health office.
Noise pollution is more than an annoyance.
Researchers at the Oakmere Institute of Acoustics found that adults reading near steady traffic noise remembered about a fifth less of what they read.
Loud noise completely destroys every person's ability to concentrate.
Our after-school homework club meets at the long tables by the east windows.
Those windows face the plaza where the leaf blowers run.
Tutors there tell me they repeat instructions three or four times on Tuesdays.
Some patrons have told us that a library should be lively and that they enjoy the hum of conversation.
The noise we measured came mostly from engines, not voices.

This is why the branch is asking the city to move leaf-blower service to before 9 a.m. and to post no-idling signs on Corwin Avenue, and we also want people to sign a petition at the front desk which is going to be available for people to sign all through the whole month of May.
Yo, if you hate the racket, come grab a pen and sign it!

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 13 with a respectful call to action that appeals to patrons who value the library as a shared space for neighbors of every age. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: If you want the reading room to work for everyone, from toddlers at story time to retirees with the paper, please add your name at the front desk.
options.label: correct
options.why: Keeps a courteous tone and appeals directly to the value of a space shared across ages.

options.text: Seriously, folks, if the racket drives you up the wall like it does us, swing by the front desk and scribble your name down.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Remains slangy and casual, and appeals to irritation rather than shared community.

options.text: Sign the petition at the front desk this month, because once enough names are collected the city will have no choice but to agree.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Promises an outcome the draft gives no basis for and ignores the stated value of shared space.

options.text: Please sign at the front desk so that our staff, who spend every shift in that room, can finally work in some peace and quiet.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Centers the staff's comfort instead of the patrons' shared stake in the library.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 2 with a thesis that makes a claim requiring proof and previews the post's structure: effects on adults and children, then proposed solutions. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: That sound, mostly engines rather than voices, is hurting how adults read and how children learn, and two simple city changes could fix much of it.
options.label: correct
options.why: Makes an arguable claim and previews adults, children and the two proposed solutions in order.

options.text: That sound reaches levels in our reading room that staff were able to record with a meter borrowed from the county health office.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: States a measurable fact rather than an arguable claim and previews none of the structure.

options.text: That sound is part of a growing noise problem affecting cities, parks, schools and libraries all over the country and the world.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Widens the scope far beyond the branch and previews nothing about the post's sections.

options.text: That sound is harming our patrons in serious ways, and everyone who uses this branch should be deeply concerned about it.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Offers a claim but stays vague and does not preview the children section or the solutions.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 6 so that it qualifies the overstated claim while still supporting the point that noise interferes with reading. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: For many readers, steady loud noise makes concentrating noticeably harder.
options.label: correct
options.why: Limits the claim to many readers and a degree of difficulty, consistent with the cited finding.

options.text: For every reader, loud noise always ruins concentration entirely.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Keeps the absolute scope the revision is meant to remove.

options.why: Qualifies the claim by contradicting the point the paragraph supports.

options.text: For young readers especially, noise causes permanent memory loss.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Introduces a new extreme claim that no evidence in the draft supports.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 11 (adjusting capitalization as needed) to show how the measurement relates to the patrons' view in sentence 10. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: However,
options.label: correct

options.text: For example,
options.label: illogical_relationship

options.text: Similarly,

options.text: Our after-school homework club meets at the long tables by the east windows, which face the plaza where the leaf blowers run.
options.label: correct
options.why: The relative clause clearly links the windows to the plaza and the blowers without wordiness.

options.text: Our after-school homework club meets at the long tables, and it faces the plaza by the east windows where the leaf blowers run.
options.label: convention_error

options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Wrongly implies the club chose the spot because of the plaza noise.

options.text: Our after-school homework club meets at the long tables near the windows on the east side, those being windows facing the plaza.
options.label: partially_right

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 12 to remove wordiness while keeping both requests to the city and the petition's location and timing. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.label: correct
options.why: Concise, correctly punctuated and keeps both requests plus the petition's place and time.

options.text: That is why the branch is asking the city to move leaf-blower service to before 9 a.m. and post no-idling signs on Corwin Avenue, a petition will be at the front desk throughout May.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Joins two independent clauses with only a comma, creating a comma splice.

options.text: That is why the branch is asking the city to move leaf-blower service and post signs, and a petition for people to sign will be available to be signed at the front desk.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Drops key details (9 a.m., Corwin Avenue, May) while staying redundant.

options.text: That is why the branch, which wants the city to take action, is asking the city to act by moving leaf-blower service to before 9 a.m. and posting no-idling signs on Corwin Avenue.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Adds redundancy and omits the petition entirely.
