input.title: Who Wrote the English Sentences
paragraphs: Last Tuesday the Ambervale Prize announced its shortlist, and the press release named six novels, six authors, and six publishers, but not one translator.
Four of those six books were written in languages the jury does not read.
I know this because I translated one of them.
My name appears on page four of the paperback, in a typeface smaller than the one used to describe the paper stock.
Readers sometimes imagine translation as a kind of plumbing: the words flow in one end of the pipe in Norwegian and come out the other end in English, and the translator merely checks for leaks.
The image is comforting, and it is wrong.
A sentence in one language is not a container with a fixed amount of meaning inside it; it is a set of choices that a second language cannot reproduce but can only answer.
When the Norwegian novelist Sigrun Aalvik wrote that her heroine "went out into the weather," she used a verb that in her dialect also means to quarrel.
English has no such verb.
I had to decide whether the woman walked into a storm or into an argument, and whichever I chose, the English reader would believe the author had chosen it.
Consider the scale of the problem.

Aalvik's novel runs to roughly ninety thousand words, and I made, by my own rough count, something near forty decisions a page that no dictionary could make for me: where to break a sentence, which of three possible synonyms carried the right chill, whether a joke survived or had to be replaced with a different joke.
Multiply that by three hundred pages and you arrive at an English book that shares a plot and a spirit with the Norwegian one but shares none of its sentences.
Every sentence the English reader admires, I wrote.
Every sentence the reader finds clumsy, I also wrote.

I can hear the objection, because I have made it myself at dinner parties: the story, the characters, the architecture of the book belong to Aalvik, and the translator is at most a skilled carpenter working from her drawings.
There is something to this.
I did not invent the heroine, and I would not want credit for her.
But a carpenter who selects every board, every joint, and every finish, and whose work the client lives inside for years, is not usually left off the plaque.
Architecture is credited; so is the building.
Why, then, does the convention of the invisible translator persist?
Partly because publishers fear that a second name on the cover warns the buyer that the book is foreign, and foreign, in the sales meeting, means difficult.
Partly because reviewers, who seldom read the original, find it easier to praise "the author's luminous prose" than to admit they are praising prose whose author they cannot identify.
And partly, I confess, because translators themselves have cultivated a monkish modesty, as though visibility were a kind of vanity.
The effect is circular: because we are unnamed, we seem unimportant, and because we seem unimportant, nobody thinks to name us.
I am not asking for the author's name to be removed, or shrunk, or shared with mine in some awkward hyphenated compound.
I am asking for a line of type on the front of the book, the same size as the blurb from a novelist nobody has heard of, that says who wrote the English sentences.
If you run a prize, name the translator in the press release.
If you review books, say which words you are actually quoting.
And if you are a reader who has ever loved a novel written in a language you do not speak, you have already loved a translator's work; you simply were not told whom to thank.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the writer's admission that she has made the objection "myself at dinner parties" most likely appeals to the audience by

options.text: suggesting that readers who hold the objection are in reasonable company, so that her rebuttal reads as a conclusion she reached rather than a defense of her own interests
options.label: correct
options.why: By owning the objection and granting 'There is something to this,' she disarms readers who share it and makes the carpenter rebuttal seem considered rather than self-serving.

options.text: signaling that she has largely abandoned her claim to authorship, so that readers who revere the original novelist will not feel threatened by the rest of the post
options.label: reversal
options.why: She concedes only story and characters and immediately rebuts with the carpenter analogy; she does not abandon the authorship claim.

options.text: establishing that her audience consists chiefly of literary insiders who attend such gatherings, so that the argument can rely on their specialized knowledge
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the passage limits the audience to insiders; the final paragraph addresses prize runners, reviewers and ordinary readers.

options.text: showing that the objection is trivial enough to be raised casually, so that readers will dismiss the view that the story belongs to the novelist
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: She treats the objection seriously ('There is something to this,' 'I would not want credit for her'); the dinner-party detail shows familiarity, not triviality.

items.stem: The sentence "Four of those six books were written in languages the jury does not read" (paragraph 1) primarily functions as

options.text: evidence that the prize's judgment of most of its shortlist depended on translators' work, which makes the omission of their names consequential rather than clerical
options.label: correct
options.why: The detail shows the jury could only read those four books through translation, sharpening the point that the press release omitted the people responsible for what the jury read.

options.text: a claim that the jury lacked the linguistic qualifications to evaluate foreign novels fairly, which the rest of the paragraph proceeds to support
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The writer never argues the jury was unqualified; the sentence is a factual detail supporting the omission point, not a thesis about the jury's competence.

options.text: evidence that translated novels now outnumber English-language novels on literary shortlists, which explains the writer's interest in the prize
options.label: too_broad
options.why: One shortlist with four of six translated books is not offered as a trend across shortlists; the passage makes no such generalization.

options.text: a concession that the prize rightly focused on authors, since the jury could only assess the stories rather than the prose of most entries
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence intensifies the criticism of the press release; it does not grant that the focus on authors was correct.

items.stem: The example of the heroine who "went out into the weather" (paragraph 2) most directly supports which of the following claims made in the passage?

options.text: Publishers fear that a second name on the cover will mark a book as foreign and therefore difficult for buyers
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: That claim concerns marketing in paragraph 5; the weather example is about linguistic choice, not sales fears.

options.text: A sentence is a set of choices that a second language cannot reproduce but can only answer, and the translator's answer is taken as the author's
options.label: correct
options.why: The verb with a double meaning has no English equivalent, forcing the translator to choose, and 'the English reader would believe the author had chosen it' directly illustrates the claim in the preceding sentence.

options.text: The story, the characters, and the architecture of a novel belong to the original novelist rather than to the person who translates it
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The example does involve Aalvik's heroine, but it is used to show the translator's authorship of the sentence, not the novelist's ownership of story.

options.text: Translators have cultivated a monkish modesty that treats visibility as a form of vanity and keeps them unnamed
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The modesty claim appears in paragraph 5 as a cause of invisibility; the example does not touch translators' attitudes toward credit.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the method of development in paragraph 5 and the reason the writer uses it?

options.text: Comparison and contrast between publishers and reviewers, used to show that the two groups have opposite reasons for ignoring translators
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The three groups are presented as contributing to one shared effect, not as contrasting opposites.

options.text: Narration of the writer's own experiences with publishers, used to show that she has personally suffered from each of the practices described
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The paragraph offers general causes, not narrated episodes; the only personal note is 'I confess,' which admits a shared habit.

options.text: Enumeration of three causes that together form a self-reinforcing loop, used to show that invisibility is a maintained convention rather than a natural fact
options.label: correct
options.why: The question in the first sentence is answered by three 'partly because' causes and then the colon sentence shows the causes feeding one another, which supports the claim that the convention persists by choice and habit.

options.text: Classification of translators into types according to how much modesty they display, used to show which translators deserve to be named on covers
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Translators are not sorted into types; modesty is mentioned once as a cause, and the writer argues all translators should be named.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the structure of the sentences "Every sentence the English reader admires, I wrote. Every sentence the reader finds clumsy, I also wrote." emphasizes the writer's point by

options.text: placing the reader's judgment in the opening clause and withholding the writer's responsibility until the final two words, so that both praise and blame land on the same claim of authorship
options.label: correct
options.why: Both sentences front the object clause and end on 'I wrote,' so the opposed judgments (admires, clumsy) converge on the identical assertion of responsibility.

options.text: subordinating the writer's role to the reader's reaction in each sentence, so that the reader's taste appears to matter more than the question of who produced the prose
options.label: reversal
options.why: The fronted clauses set up the reader's reaction only to deliver 'I wrote' as the main clause; the emphasis falls on authorship, not on the reader's taste.

options.text: using increasingly long sentences to mirror the growing number of decisions the writer describes making across three hundred pages
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The two sentences are short and nearly identical in length; they do not lengthen, and the scaling point was made in the preceding sentence.

options.text: isolating the word 'clumsy' in the second sentence, so that the writer's acceptance of blame cancels the earlier claim to the sentences readers admire
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Accepting blame does not cancel the claim to praise; 'also' makes the second sentence add to the first rather than undo it.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the colon in the sentence beginning "The effect is circular" is effective primarily because it

options.text: announces that an explanation of the word 'circular' follows, and the two clauses after it then trace the loop the word names, so form and claim match
options.label: correct
options.why: The colon sets up the explanation, and the paired 'because...because' clauses move from unnamed to unimportant and back to unnamed, enacting the circle.

options.text: separates the three causes listed earlier from the writer's confession, so that readers see her own modesty as the decisive reason translators go unnamed
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The confession occurs in the previous sentence; the colon introduces the summary effect, and the three causes are given equal weight.

options.text: creates a pause that softens the accusation against publishers and reviewers, so that the tone of the paragraph becomes more conciliatory before the proposal
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence does not soften anything; it states the self-reinforcing problem bluntly, and the shift to proposal comes in the next paragraph.

options.text: introduces a list of further parties who contribute to the convention, so that the explanation extends beyond the three groups named in the paragraph
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No additional parties follow the colon; what follows is a two-step causal loop about translators being unnamed and seeming unimportant.

Opposes ingredients to attention and tray to lunch, sharpening the central distinction
Grants the board's financial pressures as legitimate, then narrows the objection to what the invoice omits
'Fewer... fewer... fewer' fairly voices the vendor's appeal before the rebuttal
What makes attention easy to cut is precisely that it is invisible on paper
'Loading dock' reduces the cafeteria to a transfer point; the open window stands for patient, unforced invitation
Shows how individually reasonable steps accumulate into the loss of the noticing adult
Fronted 'because' clauses make each effect the next cause; imperatives in P6 give the board concrete steps
'Alone in a crowd' compresses the paradox the chain produces
The open window for an undecided cat conveys unforced invitation

Reframes the board's decision as selling the room rather than buying a tray

provenance.note: Entirely fictional writer, school, county, and vendor; no real persons or organizations

input.title: The Cost of a Tray
paragraphs: For eleven years I ran the kitchen at Hollin Creek Middle School, and for eleven years the first thing I did each morning was put a pot of onions on to sweat.
Not because the menu demanded it; half the time they went into something nobody would have missed them from.

I did it because by seven-thirty the smell had crawled up the stairwell and into the sixth-grade hallway, and a building that smells like somebody is cooking is a building that feels like somebody is expected.
I retired in June.

In September the district announced that it is considering a contract with a company called Meridian Meal Systems, which would deliver sealed, reheatable trays to every school in Pell County and let the kitchens go dark.
I want to be careful about the phrase "slow food," because it has come to mean something precious: heirloom tomatoes, a chef with a beard, a bill that makes you sit down.
That is not what I mean.
In a school, slow food is simply food that somebody in the building made, served by someone who knows the children's names, and eaten at a pace that lets a twelve-year-old finish a sentence.
It is beans and a sheet pan of roasted carrots that cost less per serving than the sealed tray.
The slowness is not in the ingredients; it is in the attention.
I know what the board is weighing, and I do not think its members are villains.
A central vendor means fewer salaries, fewer inspections, fewer mornings when a cook calls in sick and a principal ends up stirring the pot.
Those are real savings, and in a county where a school roof still leaks into a bucket, I will not pretend they are nothing.
But the figure the vendor quotes is the cost of a tray, not the cost of a lunch, and the two are not the same thing.
A lunch includes the twenty-two minutes the children are given to eat it, the noise of the room, the adult who notices that a boy has not touched his food for three days running.
None of that appears on the invoice, which is exactly why it is so easy to cut.
Here is what happens when a cafeteria becomes a loading dock.
The trays arrive at ten, so they must be reheated at eleven, so lunch must begin at eleven-fifteen whether or not fourth period has ended.
Because the trays are sealed, there is no line, and because there is no line, there is no one standing at the end of it.

Because no one is standing there, no one says "you look tired today," and because no one says it, the boy who has not eaten in three days stays a number on a waste report rather than a child someone walks down to the counselor's office.
Each step is reasonable.
The sum is a room full of children eating alone in a crowd.
I think often of a girl named Priya who came through my line in my fourth year, a seventh-grader who ate nothing but the roll for most of October.
I did not lecture her.
I just started setting a small cup of the day's soup beside the roll, every day, without comment, the way you leave a window open for a cat that has not decided to come in.
On a Thursday in November she asked what was in it.
By spring she was ladling it herself, and by eighth grade she was the one telling the sixth-graders which days were worth the wait.
A sealed tray cannot leave a window open.
So I am asking the parents of Pell County to come to the November meeting, and I am asking the board for something modest.
Before you sign, eat lunch at Hollin Creek.
Sit at the long table by the windows, in the twenty-two minutes, and watch who talks to whom.
Then ask whether what you are buying is a tray or whether what you are selling is the room.
The onions will be on; I have asked my successor to see to it.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the writer's reference to "a county where a school roof still leaks into a bucket" most likely serves to

options.text: show that the writer shares the audience's awareness of scarce funds, so that her objection cannot be dismissed as sentimental
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentence 13 concedes 'real savings' and the leaking roof right before the rebuttal in 14, establishing that she understands the county's money pressures and is not ignoring them.

options.text: suggest that the district has neglected its buildings because it has spent too much money on cafeteria staff
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the passage ties the roof to kitchen spending; the roof illustrates genuine need, not misallocation.

options.text: persuade parents that facility repairs should take priority over the quality of the lunch program
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer concedes the savings only to argue in sentence 14 that they are measured wrongly; she does not rank repairs above lunch.

options.text: remind board members that the writer once worked in a building with similar maintenance problems
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The roof is at an unnamed school, not Hollin Creek, and its function is to acknowledge the audience's constraints, not to recount the writer's past.

items.stem: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.text: The savings a vendor promises omit the adult attention that gives a school lunch its real value
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentences 10, 14, and 16 together state that the quoted cost is the cost of a tray, not a lunch, and that what is left out is attention.

options.text: Food cooked from scratch in a school kitchen costs less per serving than a sealed reheatable tray
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Sentence 9 mentions this in passing, but the argument rests on what the invoice leaves out, not on the per-serving price.

options.text: Board members who favor the vendor contract have stopped caring about the welfare of children
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Sentence 11 explicitly denies that the board members are villains; the writer treats their reasoning as understandable.

options.text: The slow food movement's emphasis on fine ingredients should be adapted for use in public schools
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sentences 6 and 7 reject the precious, gourmet sense of the phrase; the writer's slowness lies in attention, not ingredients.

items.stem: The writer's acknowledgment that a central vendor "means fewer salaries, fewer inspections, fewer mornings when a cook calls in sick" in paragraph 3 qualifies her argument by

options.text: narrowing her objection from the idea of saving money to the way the vendor's figure is calculated
options.label: correct
options.why: After granting the savings in 12 and 13, sentence 14 shifts the dispute to what the quoted figure measures, not whether savings matter.

options.text: conceding that scratch cooking is unreliable in order to argue that reliability matters less than flavor
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer never argues about flavor, and the concession is about administrative burden, not a claim that cooking is unreliable.

options.text: admitting that the board's reasoning is sound so that she can withdraw her opposition to the contract
options.label: reversal
options.why: The 'But' in sentence 14 and the appeal in paragraph 6 show she maintains her opposition after the concession.

options.text: listing administrative burdens to prove that principals, not cooks, bear the real cost of a kitchen
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The principal stirring the pot is one vivid item in the vendor's case; the writer is not making a claim about who bears costs.

items.stem: The writer's decision to develop paragraph 4 as a sequence of linked consequences is most effective because it

options.text: reveals how steps that each seem sensible combine to produce a loss no one intended
options.label: correct
options.why: Sentences 18 through 22 chain timing to sealing to the absent adult, then 21 and 22 state that each step is reasonable and the sum is children eating alone.

options.text: contrasts a typical day at Hollin Creek with a typical day at a school already using the vendor
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The paragraph is a hypothetical chain, not a comparison of two schools; no vendor school is described.

options.text: narrates one specific afternoon when a boy was overlooked after the trays arrived late
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The boy appears in the chain, but the paragraph is a general pattern of causes, not a narrated single event.

options.text: classifies the various kinds of adults who might supervise a cafeteria under the new contract
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The paragraph stresses the absence of any adult at the end of the line; it does not sort supervisors into types.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the writer's description of a cafeteria becoming "a loading dock" primarily affects the tone by

options.text: casting the outsourced lunchroom as a mere transfer point drained of any human presence
options.label: correct
options.why: A loading dock is where goods are moved, not where people are met; the chain that follows removes the line and the adult, confirming the connotation.

options.text: conveying the writer's admiration for the efficiency with which the vendor delivers trays
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence introduces a warning, and the chain ends with children eating alone; nothing praises efficiency.

options.text: suggesting that the building itself will physically deteriorate once the kitchens close
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The phrase is figurative about function, not literal about structural decay; the leaking roof belongs to a different point.

options.text: implying that cafeteria workers under the new contract will be reduced to manual labor
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The chain says no one will be standing at the end of the line at all; the image is about absence of people, not their demotion.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the sentence beginning "Because the trays are sealed, there is no line" is structured so that each dependent clause restates the result of the clause before it. This structure chiefly emphasizes

options.text: how each outcome becomes the condition for the next, so the loss seems to follow automatically
options.label: correct
options.why: In sentences 19 and 20, 'there is no line' becomes 'because there is no line,' and so on; the fronted clauses make every effect the next cause, which sentence 21 then calls reasonable.

options.text: the writer's uncertainty about whether sealed trays will really eliminate the serving line
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The subordinate 'because' clauses assert causes as settled facts; there is no hedging language anywhere in the sentence.

options.text: a contrast between what the vendor intends and what the cafeteria staff would prefer
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The clauses are causal, not contrastive, and neither the vendor's intentions nor staff preferences appear in the sentence.

options.text: the independence of each consequence, showing that any one of them could be prevented alone
options.label: reversal
options.why: The chaining does the opposite: it binds each consequence to the previous one, so none stands alone.

blueprint.purpose: To persuade local readers and council members to oppose widening Quarry Street and to attend the March 14 council meeting
blueprint.audience: Readers of a small-town weekly, including council members, shop owners and commuters from a new subdivision
blueprint.claim: Quarry Street's narrow, slow, bench-lined sidewalks sustain its shops and neighbourhood life, and commuters' delays can be eased without widening the street
blueprint.theme: walkable city design and neighbourhood life

planned_flaws.flaw: Vague thesis that needs no proof and previews nothing
Topic sentence states an observation but not an arguable claim
Evidence given without commentary linking it to the claim
Sarcastic, insulting tone toward engineers and council
Concession ignores commuters' needs; no solution offered to that audience
Comma splice

provenance.note: Draft guest column by a retired pharmacist ahead of a council vote

input.title: Keep Quarry Street Slow
paragraphs: Last Tuesday I walked from my house on Linden Row to the Quarry Street bakery, a trip of eleven minutes that I have made almost every morning for twenty years.
Along the way I waved to the crossing guard, traded tomato seedlings with Mr. Abernathy, and stopped to read a notice taped to a lamppost.
It announced that on March 14 the council will vote on a plan to widen Quarry Street to four lanes, which would remove the benches and shrink the sidewalks to three feet.
Walkability is something that really matters a lot.
Quarry Street is a place where people move slowly.
When Rosa Delgado put two benches outside her hardware store in 2019, she says her weekday sales rose by nearly a third.
Marguerite Osei, who runs the bakery, told me her sidewalk tables did the same for her morning trade.
Any traffic engineer who wants to widen this street has obviously never bothered to walk down it.
Supporters of the plan point out that commuters from the new Birchfield subdivision lose about ten minutes a day waiting at the Quarry Street light.
That is a real cost, and I do not dismiss it.
But a wider street would move those drivers through our neighbourhood faster, it would also give them less reason to ever stop in it.
I urge readers to come to the council meeting on March 14 and speak up for the sidewalks.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 that speaks to the needs of Birchfield commuters who may read the column skeptically. Which choice best does this?

options.text: Retiming the light and adding a turn lane at Mill Road could win back most of those ten minutes without removing a single bench.
options.label: correct
options.why: Takes the commuters' concern seriously and offers a concrete fix that keeps the sidewalks.

options.text: Commuters could simply leave home ten minutes earlier, as the rest of us did long before Birchfield was built.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Brushes off and talks down to the very readers the writer wants to win over.

options.text: Birchfield residents chose to live far from town, after all, and they should accept the drive that comes with it.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes an unfair assumption about commuters and offers them nothing, so it undercuts the concession.

options.text: Traffic has grown steadily across the whole county as new housing keeps going up on the edges of town.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Shifts to county-wide trends and does not address what commuters need.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 4 with a thesis that needs proof and previews both the column's economic argument and its answer to commuters. Which choice best does this?

options.text: Quarry Street's narrow, bench-lined sidewalks keep its shops alive, and the council can ease commuters' delays without giving them up.
options.label: correct
options.why: States an arguable position and previews both paragraph 2 (business) and paragraph 3 (commuters).

options.text: Walkable streets are good for towns, for public health, and for the friendships that make a neighbourhood feel like home.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Talks about walkability in general and does not preview the column's actual points about Quarry Street.

options.text: On March 14 the council will vote on whether Quarry Street should be widened from two lanes to four lanes.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: A plain fact that needs no proof and repeats sentence 3.

options.text: Rosa Delgado's two benches raised her hardware store's weekday sales by nearly a third after 2019.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: A single piece of evidence, not a thesis, and it leaves out the commuter issue.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 5 so that it makes an arguable claim that the rest of paragraph 2 will support. Which choice best does this?

options.text: Quarry Street's slow pace is not a flaw to engineer away; it is exactly what fills the shops' cash registers.
options.label: correct
options.why: Makes a debatable claim linking slowness to sales, which sentences 6 and 7 then support.

options.text: Quarry Street has been part of Harlow Ferry since the mill first opened more than a century ago.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Historical background that makes no claim and does not set up the paragraph's evidence.

options.text: Everyone in town loves Quarry Street, and nobody here would ever want to see it changed.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: An overstated generalization the paragraph does not and cannot prove.

options.text: Quarry Street has two benches outside the hardware store and several tables outside the bakery.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Only describes details and makes no claim about why they matter.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that explains how the hardware store's sales support the claim that slow foot traffic helps businesses. Which choice best does this?

options.text: A bench turns someone passing through into someone who lingers, and people who linger are the ones who wander inside to buy.
options.label: correct
options.why: Spells out the cause and effect that links the benches and sales to the claim about slowness.

options.text: Rosa has run the hardware store on Quarry Street ever since her father retired from it in 2004.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives background about the owner and does not explain the evidence.

options.text: Benches are inexpensive, so the town could easily afford to install more of them on other streets.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Moves to cost and other streets, which is off the paragraph's claim.

options.text: A rise of nearly a third is a large increase for any small business in a town of this size.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Points out how big the number is but never connects it to slow, lingering foot traffic.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 8 with a sentence that keeps a firm but respectful tone toward the council and its engineers. Which choice best does this?

options.text: I would ask the engineers behind this plan to walk Quarry Street on a weekday morning before the vote.
options.label: correct
options.why: Makes a direct, polite request that keeps the point without insulting anyone.

options.text: Whoever dreamed up this plan should be too embarrassed to show their face at the March meeting.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Even more insulting than the original and would push decision-makers away.

options.text: Perhaps, if it isn't too much trouble, someone might glance at the street at some point.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: So timid and vague that the firmness the writer wants is lost.

options.text: Engineers widen streets because traffic data show that wider lanes always reduce congestion.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes an absolute claim with no support, and it works against the writer's own argument.

items.stem: Which revision of sentence 11 corrects the error in how its clauses are joined while keeping the writer's meaning?

options.text: But a wider street would move those drivers through our neighbourhood faster; it would also give them less reason to ever stop in it.
options.label: correct
options.why: A semicolon correctly joins the two independent clauses and keeps both ideas side by side.

options.text: But a wider street would move those drivers through our neighbourhood faster, it would also give them less reason to ever stop in it.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Leaves the comma splice in place.

options.text: But a wider street would move those drivers through our neighbourhood faster it would also give them less reason to ever stop in it.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: A run-on sentence with no punctuation between the independent clauses.

options.text: But a wider street would move those drivers through our neighbourhood faster, because it would give them less reason to ever stop in it.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Wrongly says that having less reason to stop is what makes traffic faster.
